{{short description|Conditional Poisson distribution restricted to positive integers}}
{{refimprove|date=August 2013}}

In [[probability theory]], the '''zero-truncated Poisson distribution''' ('''ZTP distribution''') is a certain [[discrete probability distribution]] whose support is the set of positive integers.  This distribution is also known as the '''conditional Poisson distribution'''<ref name="cohen_clifford">{{cite journal |last=Cohen |first=A. Clifford|date=1960 |title=Estimating parameters in a conditional Poisson distribution |journal=Biometrics|volume=16|issue=2|pages=203–211|doi=10.2307/2527552|jstor=2527552}}</ref> or the '''positive Poisson distribution'''.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Singh |first=Jagbir|date=1978 |title=A characterization of positive Poisson distribution and its application |journal=SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics|volume=34|pages=545–548|doi=10.1137/0134043}}</ref> It is the conditional [[probability distribution]] of a [[Poisson distribution|Poisson-distributed]] [[random variable]], given that the value of the random variable is not zero. Thus it is impossible for a ZTP random variable to be zero. Consider for example the random variable of the number of items in a shopper's basket at a supermarket checkout line.  Presumably a shopper does not stand in line with nothing to buy (i.e., the minimum purchase is 1 item), so this phenomenon may follow a ZTP distribution.<ref>{{cite web
  |url=http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/dae/ztp.htm
  |title=Stata Data Analysis Examples: Zero-Truncated Poisson Regression
  |publisher=[[UCLA]] Institute for Digital Research and Education
  |access-date=7 August 2013
  |archive-date=29 January 2014
  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140129165838/http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/dae/ztp.htm
  |url-status=dead
  }}</ref>

Since the ZTP is a [[truncated distribution]] with the truncation stipulated as {{math|<var>k</var> > 0}}, one can derive the [[probability mass function]] {{math|<var>g</var>(<var>k</var>;<var>&lambda;</var>)}} from a standard Poisson distribution {{math|<var>f</var>(<var>k</var>;<var>&lambda;</var>}}) as follows:
<ref>{{cite book |last1=Johnson |first1=Norman L. |last2=Kemp |first2=Adrianne W.|last3=Kotz|first3=Samuel|date=2005 |title=Univariate Discrete Distributions |location=Hoboken, NJ |publisher=Wiley-Interscience |edition=third }}</ref>

: <math>g(k;\lambda) = P(X = k \mid X > 0) = 
\frac{f(k;\lambda)}{1-f(0;\lambda)} = 
\frac{\lambda ^ k e^{- \lambda} }{k ! \left ( 1 - e^{- \lambda} \right )} = \frac{\lambda^k}{(e^\lambda-1)k!}</math>

The [[expected value|mean]] is

: <math> \operatorname{E}[X]=\frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}=\frac{\lambda e^\lambda}{e^\lambda-1} </math>

and the [[variance]] is

: <math> \operatorname{Var}[X]=\frac{\lambda+\lambda^2}{1-e^{-\lambda}} - \frac{\lambda^2 }{(1-e^{-\lambda})^2} = \operatorname{E}[X](1+\lambda-\operatorname{E}[X])</math>

== Parameter estimation ==
The [[Method of moments (statistics)|method of moments]] estimator <math>\widehat{\lambda}</math> for the parameter <math>\lambda</math> is obtained by solving

: <math> \frac{\widehat{\lambda}}{1-e^{-\widehat{\lambda}}} = \bar{x} </math>

where <math>\bar{x}</math> is the [[sample mean]].<ref name="cohen_clifford"/>

This equation has a solution in terms of the [[Lambert W function]]. In practice, a solution may be found using numerical methods.

== Examples ==

== Generating zero-truncated Poisson-distributed random variables ==
Random variables sampled from the zero-truncated Poisson distribution may be achieved using algorithms derived from Poisson distribution sampling algorithms.<ref>{{cite web |last=Borje |first=Gio |title=Zero-Truncated Poisson Distribution Sampling Algorithm| url=http://giocc.com/zero_truncated_poisson_sampling_algorithm.html |date=2016-06-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180826164029/http://giocc.com/zero_truncated_poisson_sampling_algorithm.html |archive-date=2018-08-26 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

 '''init''':
     '''Let''' k ← 1, t ← ''e''<sup>−λ</sup> / (1 - ''e''<sup>−λ</sup>) * λ, s ← t.
     Generate uniform random number u in [0,1].
 '''while''' s < u '''do''':
     k ← k + 1.
     t ← t * λ / k.
     s ← s + t.
 '''return''' k.

The cost of the procedure above is linear in {{Var|k}}, which may be large for large values of <math>\lambda</math>. Given access to an efficient sampler for non-truncated Poisson random variates, a non-iterative approach involves sampling from a truncated [[exponential distribution]] representing the time of the first event in a [[Poisson point process]], conditional on such an event existing.<ref>
{{cite mailing list |url=https://stat.ethz.ch/pipermail/r-help/2005-May/070678.html
  |title=[R] simulate zero-truncated Poisson distribution
  |date=1 May 2005 |access-date=27 May 2022 |mailing-list=r-help |last=Hardie |first=Ted}}</ref>
A simple [[Python (programming language)|Python]] implementation with [[NumPy]] is:
<syntaxhighlight lang="python">
def sample_zero_truncated_poisson(rate):
    u = np.random.uniform(np.exp(-rate), 1)
    t = -np.log(u)
    return 1 + np.random.poisson(rate - t)
</syntaxhighlight>
